domains.title: Kami of Rice, Fertility, and Foxes
domains.subtitle: Guardian of the Harvest and Merchant Prosperity
domains.lead: Inari is one of the most widely worshipped kami in Japan. Originally a deity of rice and agriculture, Inari became over the centuries a patron of fertility, sake, swordsmiths, merchants, and worldly success. The vermillion torii gates and fox statues of Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyōto are among the most iconic images of Japanese religion.

cards.name: Rice and Harvest
cards.desc: Inari governs the rice plant, the foundation of the Japanese diet and economy.

cards.name: Fox Messengers
cards.desc: Kitsune serve Inari, acting as omens, guardians, and intermediaries.

cards.name: Merchant Success

mythology.lead: Inari has no single canonical myth. The kami's identity is distributed across agricultural rites, local shrine legends, and the fox lore of the Edo period.

myths.title: Deity of the Rice Plant
myths.text: Inari was first worshipped as the spirit of the rice plant itself. The Nihon Shoki records that an Inari shrine was established in 711 CE at the request of the clan head Hata no Irogu, making it one of the oldest documented shrines in Japan. Rice, sake, and fertility remained at the center of Inari devotion.

myths.title: The Fox as Messenger
myths.text: By the medieval period, the fox (kitsune) had become Inari's principal messenger. Foxes were believed to possess magical powers, to shape-shift into human form, and to act as omens. Shrine statues often show a pair of foxes, one with a rice sheaf and one with a jewel, guarding the entrance.

myths.title: Patron of Commerce
myths.text: As Japan's cities grew, merchants and artisans adopted Inari as a patron of worldly success. Small Inari shrines appeared in shops, factories, and entertainment districts. The kami who had once protected the rice field now protected the ledger and the forge.

lore.syncretism: Inari is famously syncretic. The kami has been identified with Uka-no-Mitama, Toyouke-ōmikami, and even Buddhist figures such as Dakini-ten. Fushimi Inari houses both kami and Buddhist elements, and the cult spread through networks of branch shrines associated with trade guilds and neighborhoods. Gender, number, and identity are fluid: Inari may appear as male, female, or a couple.
lore.culturalLegacy: Fushimi Inari Taisha is one of Japan's most visited shrines, its mountain paths lined with over ten thousand torii gates. Inari shrines are found at the entrances of restaurants, shops, and homes across the country. The fox has become a global symbol of Japanese folklore, and Inari-zushi (fried tofu pouches, said to be a fox favorite) bears the kami's name.
lore.extendedMeditation: Inari teaches that the sacred is not separate from the everyday. The rice in the bowl, the fox at the shrine gate, and the merchant's account book all belong to the same divine economy. Prosperity, in Inari's world, is not greed but the abundance that allows life to continue.

sources.name: Nihon Shoki (foundation of Inari shrine, 711 CE)
Smyers, The Fox and the Jewel: Shared and Private Meanings in Contemporary Japanese Inari Worship

lore.archaeology: Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyōto is Inari's head shrine, with a vast mountain complex marked by thousands of vermillion torii gates donated by worshippers from the Edo period to the present. Archaeological and architectural study of the shrine documents the growth of the Inari cult from an agricultural kami to a national deity of commerce.
